body:
Two documents are on the table and no separate criticism was supplied, so the critical material available is what each carries against itself: the account's own doubt that the avoidance may be conflict fatigue, unequal load, or something outside the chores entirely, and the rival's own doubt that its reading can pathologize explicitness and shield a flatmate who simply does not want to do their share. Both doubts still stand, and nothing yet explains why the quiet friend withdrew.

My first decision is that the two readings are not actually rivals. One concerns the semantics of particular agreements; the other concerns what kind of household the flat is. A single flat can carry both problems, and the rival concedes as much. So I will not choose between them; I will route between them.

The most valuable thing in the rival is not its alternative diagnosis but its observation instruction: when a specification is proposed, does the withdrawing flatmate engage with its content, or pull back from the very idea of a written arrangement? The most valuable things in the account are its smallness — two or three concrete items, draft framing, a one-to-one approach with a narrow ask. These compose. The account's small trial is a cheap instrument that produces exactly the observation the rival says we need. You do not have to choose between "specify first" and "ask what the flat is first"; you can run the least identity-charged version of a specification and read it the rival's way.

I would revise the account's test, though. As stated it asks whether specified items stop recurring, but that conflates two different failures: specifications adopted and still disputed, versus specifications never adopted because someone would not engage. Recurrence tells you about ambiguity only if the specifications were actually taken up. The engagement dimension has to be added, and that dimension is precisely the rival's contribution.

I would also revise the rival's coercion claim. To the extent the worry is real, it lives less in the content of a written arrangement than in its use. A draft becomes the binding document the privacy-reading flatmate fears at the moment somebody cites it as evidence of another person's failures. What protects the draft is a rule of prospective-only use: the note records what is being tried, never who failed.

What I would not adopt is the rival's opening move — asking each flatmate separately what they take the flat to be. Not because the question is wrong, but because of its cost profile. It front-loads the most identity-charged conversation onto the least engaged participant, and it is nearly impossible to answer "three overlapping private lives" without sounding as though you are declaring you do not care about the people you live with. The same evidence is available more cheaply through the probe above. If the probe is declined, or produces pullback from the idea itself, the meaning question becomes the next move rather than the first one.

I would also temper the rival's truce arrangements. Owned zones reduce exposure, but they relocate disputes rather than ending them — to smell, pests, shared fixtures, whatever one zone does to another. A rotation under changing schedules fails exactly at the swap. Which isolates the piece that survives under both readings: the fallback clause. Whatever arrangement is tried, "what happens when you cannot do it, said in advance" is load-bearing, because schedule change is the one fact both diagnoses accept.

So the plan I would hand the reader:

Pick two or three recurring items. Specify done, by when, and the fallback. Offer it as a two-week, revocable draft all three can edit, in the least formal channel that works, and raise the smallest item one-to-one with the quiet friend. Then read two things: engagement with content versus pullback from the idea, and whether the specified items recur. Engaged and recurrence falls — keep going item by item; do not force a meaning-level conversation. Engaged but recurrence persists — the ambiguity reading weakens; now hold the rival's separate conversations about what the flat is, one at a time, without moral framing, and do not immediately fold them into a group decision. Pullback from the idea itself — the rival's reading gains weight; offer the least committal alternative, zones with a minimal boundary standard, and if even that is declined, the avoidance is about participation as such, not chores.

Throughout: never cite the note as evidence of past failure. And set the escalation threshold in advance — one proposal made, one revision offered, two weeks elapsed — so that the lease question, on which both sources converge, is raised on a calm occasion against a settled condition rather than inside a chore dispute. Both documents insist the larger decision must not be forced by an argument; a threshold fixed beforehand is what makes that insistence more than an intention.

Two limits to keep visible. First, everything arrives through one narrator. We cannot check whether "we agreed" is itself the contested memory, or whether the reader's own follow-through is part of the pattern. The cheap disciplines that follow are for the reader to hold their own specified items predictably regardless of what the others do, and for nobody to interpret the friend's silence. The privacy reading is owed uptake when stated, not inferred from absence — which is also the guard against the rival's own worry that its frame could shield someone who just does not want to do their share. Second, if the friend declines even the low-pressure one-to-one ask, this plan will have bought only the knowledge that the avoidance survives a change of format. Whether to wait longer or press the larger conversation with diminished goodwill is not something the material lets me weigh.

What this amounts to is not a diagnosis but a routing. Each step is chosen so that whichever reading is true produces a different visible outcome, without asking anyone to declare what kind of household they believe in before they have seen a concrete proposal.
